# Welcome {-}

A sample size calculation is a way of checking whether a planned study can answer its research question. Through clinical examples and interactive tools, you will explore what different studies could show, justify assumptions, and write a sample size justification.

## How to use this tutorial {-}

This tutorial is intended for both students and researchers. Students may find the core route sufficient for planning a basic two-arm clinical trial. Researchers and other readers can deepen their understanding through the advanced sections on power curves, simulation methods, precision planning and other study designs. Choose a route according to your experience and study question. Blue backgrounds identify core material; purple backgrounds advanced extensions. Advanced indicates scope beyond the basic calculations, not technical difficulty.

The core treatment comparisons use two independent groups with equal allocation and a two-sided test. Later sections consider other planning goals and designs.

You can use the activity links to open [the tutorial and matching apps together](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many). The figures and worked results also let you follow the reasoning without opening an app. For a reminder of a term, see [Key parameters and prerequisites](#glossary). If you have a project in mind, check [Where does my study fit?](#study-designs) before choosing a calculator.

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
## Core learning outcomes {#core-route .unnumbered .core-heading}

The linked sections should help you develop a sample size justification for a basic two-arm trial. By the end, you should be able to:

- [Define a clinical question and justify assumptions](#clinical-question), distinguishing the expected difference, target difference and clinical threshold.
- [Explain Type I error rate, Type II error rate and power](#power), and [interpret results using a confidence interval](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically).
- Use [one simulated study and many studies](#activity-1-one-study-then-many) to distinguish sample estimates from population parameters and see how results vary.
- [Calculate sample size for two proportions or two means](#calculations) and [adjust recruitment for expected losses](#account-for-expected-losses), distinguishing analyzable counts from recruitment counts.
- [Examine plausible alternative assumptions](#stress-test-the-study-plan), recognize [underpowered studies](#what-if-the-study-is-too-small-for-its-purpose) and assess [ways to increase power](#increase-power).
- [Write a sample size justification](#write-a-sample-size-justification) addressing evidence, feasibility and limitations, and complete the [Activity: Record and justify your assumptions](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=assumptions_report).

Before using a calculator for your own project, you should check [Where does my study fit?](#study-designs).
:::

::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
## Advanced learning outcomes {#advanced-route .unnumbered .advanced-heading}

The extensions below may be relevant to your study question. They should help you:

- Distinguish [an observed significance boundary from planned power](#critical-observed-difference) and explore [sampling distributions and error regions](#alpha-beta).
- [Read power curves](#curves) and evaluate what a fixed sample can establish.
- [Build a simulated clinical trial](#simulation) to examine power, coverage and precision, accounting for Monte Carlo uncertainty.
- Plan for [estimation](#plan-for-precision), [prevalence](#prevalence), [existing-data reuse](#dataset-reuse) or [pilot feasibility](#pilot-feasibility), including constraints in [rare diseases](#rare-diseases).
- Recognize [study designs that need another method](#study-designs), including paired measurements and prediction models.
- [Reproduce calculations and simulations](#appendix) with their assumptions and methods documented.

:::


# Introduction {#clinical-question .core-heading}



::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Explain why sample size starts with the clinical question.
- Identify the assumptions needed before calculating.
- Distinguish expected differences, target differences and clinical thresholds in a two-arm clinical trial.
:::

## The chronic pain study: how many patients do you need? {#the-chronic-pain-study-how-many-patients-do-we-need .core-heading}

Suppose you are planning a trial of a novel pain treatment against standard treatment. Does the novel treatment increase the percentage of patients reporting pain relief at four weeks?

You plan to randomly allocate patients to two independent groups of equal size. The primary outcome is pain relief at four weeks: yes or no. A small pilot found relief in 7 of 10 patients receiving the novel treatment and 3 of 10 receiving standard treatment: 70% versus 30%, an observed difference of 40 percentage points.

This looks promising, but twenty patients give you limited information. How many patients would make the main trial informative? In what follows, you will build a plan step by step, then examine what different repetitions of that study could show.

This first section focuses on two-arm randomized superiority trials. Later chapters extend the reasoning to other outcomes, estimation, existing datasets and other study designs.

You can develop a study plan alongside the tutorial, beginning with the question and evidence. Your plan should include the calculation and recruitment target, and explain how uncertain assumptions affect the recommendation. The [Activity: Record and justify your assumptions](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=assumptions_report) brings these decisions together; you can complete it gradually rather than start a new worksheet in every chapter.

## What should this study establish? {.core-heading}

A sample size calculation checks whether a planned study can answer its question. Too few patients can leave an important question unresolved; unnecessary recruitment also uses time and resources. For the pain trial, your plan should address four connected questions:

- Statistical: can the study detect a treatment benefit and estimate its size precisely enough?
- Clinical: how much additional pain relief would matter to patients?
- Ethical: does the information the study could provide justify participants' burden and risk?
- Practical: can you recruit the required patients within the available time and budget?

The final plan should address all four. A statistical target alone does not establish clinical usefulness or feasibility.

### Ethical review and the study protocol {.core-heading}

In the Netherlands, research that falls under the Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act (WMO) requires prior review and a positive decision from an accredited medical research ethics committee (METC, or MREC in English) or the CCMO before it starts [@ccmowmo]. The study protocol should explain the proposed sample size, the evidence supporting its assumptions and what the study can establish. This connects the statistical justification to the clinical question, participant burden and feasibility. When designing a study, consult the relevant review committee's requirements and the applicable [CCMO protocol template](https://english.ccmo.nl/documents/2018/09/19/standard-research-file-c1-template-research-protocol).

## What assumptions do you need before calculating? {#how-do-you-determine-the-minimum-required-sample-size .core-heading}

Before choosing numerical parameters, you should consult guidance appropriate to the study design and research question. For a randomized trial, SPIRIT 2025 for the protocol and CONSORT 2025, together with relevant extensions, for reporting the results provide relevant guidance [@spiritconsort2025]. For other designs, you should consult the corresponding guidance, such as STROBE for observational studies or STARD for diagnostic accuracy; [Where does my study fit?](#study-designs) provides routes. These are reporting guidelines: they help identify decisions to document. Then you can specify the primary outcome, the expected results in each group, the planned analysis and the acceptable error rates. Follow the question through to the analysis before choosing numbers [@fong2026; @wang2020]:

- Who are the patients, and how will treatment be allocated?
- What outcome will be measured, and at what time?
- What quantity will answer the question: here, the absolute difference in four-week relief percentages?
- Which analysis will estimate that quantity and test the hypothesis?

The map below gathers the remaining decisions. Your chronic pain plan has two independent groups, equal allocation and a binary outcome. A different question or analysis may need a different sample size method.

```{r study-questions-map, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
knitr::asis_output(render_question_map())
```

The examples use frequentist methods: two-sided significance tests for superiority and confidence intervals for estimation. Non-inferiority, equivalence and clustered trials require different hypotheses or calculations; [Where does my study fit?](#study-designs) helps identify these designs. For Bayesian planning, see [@kunzmann2021review].

## What do you expect, what will you plan for, and what matters clinically? {#what-do-we-expect-what-will-we-plan-for-and-what-matters-clinically .core-heading}

Suppose the pilot and other relevant evidence support an expected difference of 40 percentage points. For the sample size calculation, use a target difference of 30 percentage points: 60% relief with the novel treatment versus 30% with standard treatment. Separately, after consulting with patients and clinicians, you set the minimally clinically relevant difference (i.e., the clinical threshold) at 20 percentage points.

The expected difference is the anticipated population difference based on current evidence, with uncertainty. The target difference is the between-group difference used in the sample size calculation: the assumed true difference at which you evaluate power. It is not a result the study must achieve. The clinical threshold is the smallest treatment benefit judged worthwhile by patients and clinicians. These terms identify different decisions and may have the same value in a study. DELTA² guidance distinguishes realistic and important differences and explains that the target difference need not equal the smallest clinically important difference [@cook2018delta2; @lakens2022]. Event rates in this particular trial are defined as the the percentage of patients reporting pain relief at the specified four-week follow-up.

| Quantity | Value | Role in this study |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Expected difference | 40 percentage points | Best current expectation, with uncertainty |
| Target difference | 30 percentage points: 60% versus 30% | Assumed true difference at which you evaluate power |
| Clinical threshold | 20 percentage points | Smallest benefit judged worthwhile by patients and clinicians |

Table: (\#tab:pain-planning-values) Three distinct decisions for the chronic pain trial.

The three values in Table \@ref(tab:pain-planning-values) answer different questions. Using a smaller target difference acknowledges uncertainty here; subtracting a fixed amount from every pilot estimate is not a general rule. Your choice should be supported by relevant evidence and an examination of plausible alternatives. Absolute differences should be expressed in percentage points. A generic description of an effect as small, medium or large is insufficient justification [@caldwell2020].

Choosing 30 rather than 20 percentage points has a consequence: a study planned for high power at 30 will generally have lower power at a 20-point benefit, even though that smaller benefit matters clinically. For this illustration, suppose the team considers a 30-point benefit realistic and large enough to support adopting the treatment. Its plan must acknowledge that a 20-point benefit could remain inconclusive. If reliably detecting the smallest worthwhile benefit is essential, evaluate the sample required at 20 instead. Affordability alone is not a justification for choosing a larger target [@cook2018delta2].

::: {.activity}
Which target difference would you use for this trial: 20, 30 or 40 percentage points? Your explanation should identify whose judgment establishes clinical importance, what evidence makes your choice realistic, and what the choice means for smaller worthwhile benefits. These are hypothetical values; a real protocol needs outcome-specific evidence.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-target-choice">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A defensible choice in this illustration is a target difference of 30 percentage points, provided relevant evidence supports its realism and patients and clinicians consider that benefit worthwhile. The expected difference of 40 points is uncertain; it should not be used simply to obtain a smaller sample. The clinical threshold remains 20 points. Planning for 30 means accepting lower power at a worthwhile 20-point benefit. If reliably detecting that smallest worthwhile benefit is essential, 20 would be the appropriate target, with its larger sample requirement. More than one answer can be justified; the evidence, clinical judgment and intended conclusion should support the choice.

</details>
:::

The target difference should describe an absolute difference between groups. An important improvement within one patient needs to be translated into the study's outcome before it can inform this choice. For example, the criterion used to classify a patient as reporting pain relief and the smallest worthwhile difference in relief percentages between treatments are separate decisions [@cook2018delta2].

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-pilot-effect">
<summary>Common misconception: the pilot reveals the true treatment effect</summary>

The pilot's 70% versus 30% relief rates are sample estimates and could change in another small sample. They inform your expectations, but do not establish the population effect. The expected difference, target difference and clinical threshold answer different questions and should each be justified.

</details>

The pilot suggests a possible benefit, but its estimate is uncertain. It helps inform the study plan; it does not settle the clinical question. After introducing error rates and power, you can [compare the pilot result with what a larger study could establish](#critical-observed-difference).

## Record the assumptions {#record-assumptions .core-heading}

Before choosing a sample size, your study plan should distinguish what you expect, what matters clinically, and the difference used in the calculation.

| Decision | What to make explicit |
|---|---|
| Question and outcome | Population, intervention, comparator, primary outcome and time point |
| Goal | Testing, estimation, fixed resources, or a stated combination |
| Effect scale | Treatment minus control; score units or percentage points; direction of benefit |
| Expected difference | Best current expectation, supporting evidence and uncertainty |
| Clinical threshold | Smallest benefit that matters to patients, with justification |
| Target difference | Difference used in the power calculation, with justification |
| Variation or event rates | Common standard deviation or control and treatment percentages; evidence source, population and time point |
| Sensitivity | Plausible alternative differences, standard deviations or event rates; identify the least certain assumptions |
| Analysis and power | Planned test and confidence interval; sidedness, Type I error rate and target power |
| Precision | Desired full confidence interval width and confidence level |
| Allocation and counts | Allocation ratio; per-group and total analyzable sample sizes |
| Recruitment | Expected losses, recruitment target, recruitment period and available resources |
| Intended conclusion | What the design could establish and what remains uncertain |

Table: (\#tab:planning-assumptions) Assumptions to record before planning the sample size.

The target difference tells the calculation where to evaluate power. The standard deviation describes variation between individuals; the standard error describes sampling variation of an estimate. For binary outcomes, you should report each group's event rate as a percentage and their absolute difference in percentage points. [The glossary](#glossary) explains these terms.

For each numerical assumption, you should record the source, its relevance to these patients and this outcome, and a plausible range. Evidence from a different follow-up time or patient population may not transfer directly. For a clinical threshold, you should record the reasoning. DELTA² and CONSORT emphasize explaining the assumptions and calculation as opposed to reporting the final number [@cook2018delta2; @consortee2025].

::: {.activity}
Which count belongs in the protocol: analyzable patients or patients to recruit? Record both and explain the adjustment for expected losses when you complete the calculation.

You can develop your report in the [Activity: Record and justify your assumptions](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=assumptions_report). The text boxes let you build a study-plan report alongside your answers. Your clinical question and evidence come first; the sample size and recruitment counts can be added after the calculation activities. You can load a hypothetical two-arm example, save your entries, and download the report. Your report should clarify the role of the expected difference, target difference and clinical threshold, and explain what your study could establish.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-protocol-counts">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Your protocol should state both the required analyzable sample and the number you plan to recruit, with per-group and total counts clearly identified. If 60 analyzable patients are required per group and 10% are expected to be lost, the recruitment target is ceiling(60/0.90) = 67 per group, or 134 in total. This inflation aims to preserve the expected analyzable count; it does not guarantee retention or remove bias from missing outcomes. The final report should use the count from your chosen calculation method and justify the assumed loss rate.

</details>

:::


Small pilot effects are uncertain. Following up only pilots whose estimated effect gives an affordable main study can introduce additional bias [@albers2018]. A pilot can still inform recruitment, measurement procedures and variability, while providing an uncertain treatment-difference estimate. In this tutorial, you examine plausible ranges explicitly; [further planning approaches](#further-planning-approaches) address more formal ways to account for uncertainty.

::: {.activity}
Predict and justify. If the pilot had shown relief in 6 rather than 7 treated patients, should the clinical threshold change? Explain why a noisy pilot estimate and a judgment about meaningful benefit answer different questions.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-pilot-threshold">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The clinical threshold should remain 20 percentage points. Changing one pilot outcome changes the observed treatment relief from 70% to 60%, and the observed difference from 40 to 30 percentage points, with standard treatment still at 30%. It may change your expectation of the treatment difference or your assessment of its uncertainty. It does not, by itself, change what patients and clinicians regard as a worthwhile benefit. A clinical threshold needs a clinical justification, rather than following each noisy pilot estimate.

</details>
:::

<div class="core-next">Continue along the core route: <a href="#power">Power and error rates</a>.</div>

# What does statistical power tell you? {#power .core-heading}



::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Explain [Type I error rate](#alpha), [Type II error rate](#beta) and [power](#statistical-power) under a specified population scenario.
- Distinguish sample estimates from population parameters, and the outcome of one study from the performance of a design across repeated studies.
:::

Suppose you repeated the same planned study many times, with the same sample size, analysis and specified true treatment effect. Power is the percentage of those studies that would reject the null hypothesis given that the null hypothesis is false. At 90% power, about 90 out of 100 repetitions would detect that effect if it exists, while about 10 would not. This describes the design's long-run performance. You do not need to conduct the trial repeatedly: calculations or simulations estimate this probability under the stated assumptions.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-power-meaning">
<summary>Common misconception: 90% power means a 90% probability that the treatment works</summary>

Power assumes a particular true effect and describes how often the planned test would reject the null hypothesis across repeated studies. It does not tell us how likely that effect is to exist. A study with 90% power can still produce an inconclusive result.

</details>

You can now return to the planning question: if pain relief is 60% with the novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment, how often would studies of a given size detect the difference? Power describes this repeated-study performance under the specified assumptions.

## Hypotheses and error probabilities {.core-heading}

Let $\delta$ denote the population difference in percentages: novel treatment minus standard treatment. A positive difference favors the novel treatment; a negative difference favors standard treatment. The planned two-sided test asks whether this difference is zero or differs from zero in either direction.

\begin{equation}
H_0: \delta=0, \qquad H_1: \delta\ne0.
(\#eq:hypotheses)
\end{equation}

For the sample size calculation, you assume 60% relief with the novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment—a true difference of 30 percentage points. Power describes how often the planned test would find a statistically significant result under that assumption. The 30-point target is a calculation input and not a minimum difference that a significant result must demonstrate.


```{r error-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Decision = c("Reject the null", "Do not reject the null"),
  `Null is true` = c("Type I error", "Correct non-rejection"),
  `Specified alternative is true` = c("Power (1 - Type II error rate)", "Type II error"),
  check.names = FALSE), caption = "Testing decisions across repeated studies.")
```

Type I error means rejecting a true null hypothesis. Type II error means failing to reject a false null hypothesis. Power is the probability of rejection under a specified alternative, design and analysis.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-Type I error rate-meaning">
<summary>Common misconception: Type I error rate of 5% means a significant result has a 5% probability of being a false positive</summary>

Type I error rate of 5% means that the testing procedure rejects in about 5% of repetitions when the null hypothesis is true, under its assumptions. It does not give the probability that a significant result is a false positive. Type I error rate conditions on the null hypothesis being true; it does not tell us how likely that hypothesis is after observing the data.

</details>

Type I error rate of 5% and power of 80% or 90% are common planning choices. Choose and justify them in context. The error rates describe how often the test makes each kind of mistake under specified assumptions, not how serious those mistakes would be clinically. When choosing them, you should consider the consequences of recommending an ineffective treatment and of failing to detect a worthwhile benefit. A non-significant result does not show that the treatments are equivalent; the study may simply lack enough information to distinguish them.

## Activity: Chronic pain: one study and many studies {#activity-1-one-study-then-many .core-heading}

Suppose the population event rates are 30% pain relief with standard treatment and 60% with the novel treatment. In this simulation, those parameters are specified; the true population difference is 30 percentage points. Each simulated trial samples different patients, so its observed percentages and treatment difference vary. These sample estimates are not the population parameters themselves.

### A couple of individual trials {.core-heading}

With 20 patients per group, three trials from the same assumed population could give the following results:

```{r pain-sample-estimates}
example_trials <- lapply(20260941:20260943, function(trial_seed) {
  scenario <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = 20,
    p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
    seed = trial_seed)
  simulate_one_study(scenario)
})
trial_examples <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(example_trials), function(i) {
  trial <- example_trials[[i]]
  rates <- tapply(trial$data$outcome, trial$data$group, mean)
  data.frame(Trial = i, `Standard treatment: observed relief` = percent(rates["Control"]),
    `Novel treatment: observed relief` = percent(rates["Treatment"]),
    `Observed difference` = paste0(round(100 * trial$result$estimate), " percentage points"),
    `95% confidence interval` = paste0(round(100 * trial$result$lower), " to ", round(100 * trial$result$upper), " percentage points"),
    check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
knitr::kable(trial_examples, caption = "Three simulated trials with 20 patients per group, all sampled under the same 30% and 60% population event rates.")
```

The population assumptions stay the same across these trials. Their observed relief percentages, differences and confidence intervals do not. In a real trial, you observe the sample and estimate the population parameters; the simulation makes that distinction visible because its population parameters are known by construction.

### Many trials and a larger sample {.core-heading}

Repeating the trial 5,000 times shows a range of possible sample differences. The larger samples generally give estimates closer to the specified population difference, although any individual trial can still differ from it.

```{r three-samples}
sample_sizes <- c(20, 50, 80)
batches <- lapply(sample_sizes, function(n) {
  scenario <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = n,
    p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
    width_target = .20, B = 5000, seed = 20260921 + n)
  simulate_trials(scenario)
})
power_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(batches, power_row))
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Patients per group` = power_results$n_per_group,
  `Statistically significant results` = percent(power_results$simulated_power),
  check.names = FALSE), caption = "Percentage of 5,000 simulated trials detecting the assumed 30-percentage-point population difference at each sample size.")
```

```{r sample-differences, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Observed treatment differences across 5,000 simulated trials at each sample size. The dashed line marks the specified population difference of 30 percentage points. Larger samples generally produce less variable estimates.", fig.alt="Three histograms of observed relief differences with 20, 50 and 80 patients per group, showing progressively narrower distributions around the same population difference of 30 percentage points."}
local({
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  for (batch in batches) {
    hist(100 * batch$results$estimate, breaks = seq(-100, 100, 5),
      xlim = c(-40, 90), col = "#b9d4f3", border = "white",
      main = paste(batch$spec$n, "patients per group"),
      xlab = "Observed difference in relief (percentage points)", ylab = "Number of trials")
    abline(v = 30, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#69509a")
  }
})
```

Figure \@ref(fig:sample-differences) shows sampling variation; the table shows how often the planned test detects the specified population difference. The assumed true difference here equals the 30-point target difference used to evaluate power. The case's expected difference remains 40 points and its clinical threshold 20 points.

::: {.activity}
You can try [Activity: Chronic pain: one study and many studies](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many) with 20 patients per group, standard-treatment relief 30%, novel-treatment relief 60%, and Type I error rate 5%. One study, followed by another, lets you compare sample estimates with the specified population rates. Many studies shows the range of results and how often the test detects the difference. You can then compare 50 and 80 patients per group.

Which quantities stay fixed across trials, and which change? Why does a larger sample usually give a more precise estimate, while more simulation repetitions do not increase the power of each trial?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-sample-versus-population">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Within a batch of trials, the specified population relief rates stay at 30% and 60%, so their true difference stays at 30 percentage points. The sample size, allocation, analysis, Type I error rate and clinical threshold also stay fixed. The patients sampled, observed relief counts and percentages, estimated difference, confidence interval, p-value and testing decision can change from trial to trial.

A larger sample gives each trial more information, which generally reduces the sampling variation of its estimate and narrows its confidence interval. Increasing the sample size deliberately changes the design; it can also increase power at the same true effect. More simulation repetitions instead give you a more precise estimate of that design's performance, reducing Monte Carlo error. Each individual trial still has the same number of patients and the same power.

</details>

:::

This repeated-study approach follows the introductory teaching idea in @superpowerbook2022 and the use of simulation in health-sciences education [@thiesmeier2024; @rudolph2021]. The [advanced simulation explanation](#precision-of-a-simulation) covers p-value distributions, interval coverage and Monte Carlo uncertainty.

<div class="core-next">Continue along the core route: <a href="#calculations">Basic sample size calculations</a>.</div>

## Does the pilot already answer the clinical question? {#critical-observed-difference .advanced-heading}



The pilot's observed 40-percentage-point difference exceeds the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold. But the estimate is uncertain. Using a two-sided comparison of proportions gives a p-value of approximately 0.074. With a Type I error rate of 5%, this does not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis using the chosen test.

What would happen with one more response? Keep standard treatment at 3 of 10 patients, but increase novel-treatment relief from 7 to 8 of 10:

```{r pain-critical-p-values, warning=FALSE}
# Compare the pilot result with one additional treatment response
pain_p_value <- function(novel, standard, n) {
  prop.test(
    x = c(novel, standard),
    n = c(n, n),
    alternative = "two.sided",
    correct = FALSE
  )$p.value
}

round(c(
  "7 versus 3" = pain_p_value(7, 3, 10),
  "8 versus 3" = pain_p_value(8, 3, 10)
), 3)
```

```{r pain-critical-p-values-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Novel treatment` = c("7/10 (70%)", "8/10 (80%)"), `Standard treatment` = "3/10 (30%)", `Observed difference` = c("40 percentage points", "50 percentage points"), `p-value` = formatC(c(pain_p_value(7,3,10), pain_p_value(8,3,10)), format="f", digits=3), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Pilot comparisons with seven or eight responses to the novel treatment.")
```

With 8 rather than 7 patients reporting relief, the result becomes statistically significant. For this particular comparison, the smallest observed difference giving $p<0.05$ is therefore $0.8-0.3=0.5$, or 50 percentage points.

Notice that the clinical threshold remains 20 percentage points. What patients would consider a worthwhile improvement does not change because your pilot happens to contain only 10 patients per group.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-significance">
<summary>Common misconception: statistical significance decides whether a treatment matters</summary>

A non-significant result does not establish that the treatments are equally effective. A significant result does not establish that the benefit matters to patients. Examine the estimated difference and its confidence interval against both zero and the clinical threshold.

</details>

*The calculation above uses an approximate test without continuity correction, matching the [reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many). With such small groups, an exact test may give a different result.*

### What happens if you recruit more patients? {.advanced-heading}

You can repeat this calculation for larger studies. At each sample size, the observed percentage reporting relief with standard treatment stays at 30%. The calculation identifies the smallest number reporting relief with the novel treatment that gives $p<0.05$.

```{r pain-critical-effect, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=5.8, fig.cap="Smallest observed improvement giving p < 0.05 at each sample size, conditional on an observed control response of 30%. The two-sided score test uses no continuity correction. Points represent attainable patient counts; connecting lines guide the eye. The hypothetical clinical threshold is 20 percentage points. Counts are analyzable patients before adjustment for dropout.", fig.alt="The smallest observed difference giving statistical significance falls from 50 percentage points at 10 patients per group to 14 at 100 per group. A horizontal line marks the clinical threshold of 20 percentage points. The pilot difference of 40 points at 10 patients per group lies below the significance threshold."}
pain_n <- seq(10, 100, by = 10)
pain_critical <- vapply(pain_n, function(n) {
  control <- as.integer(round(0.30 * n))
  treatment <- seq.int(control + 1L, n)
  p <- vapply(treatment, function(x) pain_p_value(x, control, n), numeric(1))
  min((treatment[p < 0.05] - control) / n)
}, numeric(1))

local({
  old_par <- par(mar = c(5, 5, 2, 1), las = 1)
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  plot(pain_n, 100 * pain_critical, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2,
       col = "#17658A", ylim = c(0, 66), xaxt = "n",
       xlab = "Analyzable patients per group (equal allocation)",
       ylab = "Observed difference in pain relief (percentage points)")
  axis(1, at = pain_n)
  abline(h = 20, col = "#A5500C", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
  points(10, 40, pch = 1, cex = 1.5, lwd = 2, col = "#303A43")
  legend("topright",
         c("Smallest observed difference with p < 0.05",
           "Clinical threshold: 20 percentage points",
           "Pilot: 7/10 versus 3/10"),
         col = c("#17658A", "#A5500C", "#303A43"),
         lty = c(1, 2, NA), pch = c(16, NA, 1),
         lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
})
```

With 20 patients per group, an observed difference of 35 percentage points is sufficient for statistical significance under these conditions. With 50 patients per group, the corresponding difference is 20 percentage points. As the sample size increases, smaller observed differences can therefore become statistically significant.

Figure \@ref(fig:pain-critical-effect) shows how the observed significance boundary changes. The dashed line shows the clinically meaningful difference chosen for this example. With a larger sample, a result can be statistically significant even when the observed difference is smaller than this clinical threshold. You therefore need to consider the size of the difference and its confidence interval when interpreting the result.

### How does this relate to power? {.advanced-heading}

The significance boundary concerns an observed result. Power concerns the performance of the planned study: *If the true treatment difference is 30 percentage points, how likely is your study to produce a statistically significant result?*

Different samples will give different observed differences, even when the true treatment effect remains the same. Some will be larger and others smaller. A power calculation takes this variation into account. The [simulation activities](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many) explore this probability across repeated studies.

This illustration draws on the distinction between a critical observed effect and a sensitivity power analysis in @lakens2022, and section 1.7 of *Power Analysis with Superpower* [@superpowerbook2022].

::: {.activity}
Before continuing, consider a study that finds a statistically significant difference of 20 percentage points. What would you still need to know before deciding whether the novel treatment offers a clinically meaningful benefit?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-clinical-interpretation">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

You would need the confidence interval and a justified clinical threshold, as well as information about harms, burden and the credibility of the study. A statistically significant 20-point estimate can exclude zero while its interval still includes benefits smaller than the 20-point clinical threshold. The point estimate alone therefore does not establish that the population benefit meets or exceeds that threshold. Clinical interpretation should consider the plausible range of benefits and harms, rather than treating significance as proof of clinical importance.

</details>

:::

## See Type I error rate and Type II error rate as areas {#alpha-beta .advanced-heading}



A single-sample illustration lets you see the two error probabilities. Suppose the null mean systolic blood pressure is 120 mmHg, the specified alternative is 125 mmHg, the population SD is known to be 15 mmHg, and 25 independent observations are taken. For this one-sided known-SD illustration, rejection occurs when the sample mean exceeds a critical value. The [two-arm treatment-comparison activities](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many) use two-sided tests.

Both curves represent the sampling distribution of the sample mean, not the distribution of individual blood pressures. Their SD is the standard error, $15/\sqrt{25}=3$ mmHg. Type I error rate is the rejection area under the null curve. Under the specified alternative, Type II error rate is the non-rejection area, and power is the rejection area.

```{r alpha-beta-areas}
mu0 <- 120
mu1 <- 125
sigma <- 15
n <- 25
alpha <- .05
standard_error <- sigma / sqrt(n)
critical <- mu0 + qnorm(1 - alpha) * standard_error
beta <- pnorm(critical, mean = mu1, sd = standard_error)
c(standard_error = standard_error, critical = critical,
  beta = beta, power = 1 - beta)
```

```{r alpha-beta-areas-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Measure=c("Standard error", "Critical mean", "Type I error rate", "Type II error rate", "Power"), Result=c(paste(standard_error,"mmHg"), paste(round(critical,1),"mmHg"), percent(alpha), percent(beta), percent(1-beta))),
  caption = "Error rates and power for the specified sampling distributions.")
```

```{r sampling-distribution-figure, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Sampling distributions of the mean with 25 independent observations and known SD 15 mmHg. The shaded rejection area under the null is Type I error rate; the shaded non-rejection area under the specified alternative is Type II error rate.", fig.alt="The null curve is centered at 120 and the alternative curve at 125 mmHg. Both have standard error 3. The critical mean is about 124.9; Type I error rate is 5 percent and Type II error rate about 49 percent."}
sampling_example <- normal_sampling_operating_characteristics(
  mu0 = mu0, mu1 = mu1, sigma = sigma, n = n, alpha = alpha,
  sidedness = "greater")
plot_sample_mean_distributions(sampling_example)
```

Here the critical mean is about 124.9 mmHg and power is about 51%. Repeating the study at the specified alternative would produce a mean above that threshold about half the time. This does not mean that the alternative has a 51% probability of being true.

[Activity: Explore Type I and Type II error rates and power](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=alpha_beta). Increase n while holding the two population means and SD fixed. The curves become narrower because the standard error decreases. Explain how the rejection rule still controls Type I error rate while Type II error rate changes. Then compare one-sided and two-sided rules; sidedness should follow the research question before data collection.

## Precision of a simulation {.advanced-heading}



The following histograms count the p-values from the independent simulated studies. The dashed line marks Type I error rate. The fraction below the line estimates power under the specified alternative (Figure \@ref(fig:p-values)).

```{r p-values, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.cap="P-values from 5,000 independent clinical trials at each sample size. The proportion below Type I error rate estimates power for the assumed relief probabilities.", fig.alt="Three histograms compare p-values with 20, 50 and 80 patients per group. The numerical rejection fractions and their Monte Carlo intervals are in the preceding table."}
par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (batch in batches) plot_p_values(batch)
```

```{r simulation-monte-carlo-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(power_results,
  c("simulated_power", "MC_lower_95", "MC_upper_95")),
  caption = "Estimated power and Monte Carlo intervals for the three simulated sample sizes.")
```

Rejection rate means the percentage of simulated studies with a statistically significant result. Under a specified treatment effect it estimates power; under no treatment effect it estimates the Type I error rate. Confidence interval coverage is the percentage of intervals containing the assumed true effect. Monte Carlo uncertainty is uncertainty from using a limited number of simulated studies. The app tables pair these established terms with their practical meaning.

Use $n$ for patients per group and $B$ for the number of simulated studies. If $\hat p$ is the simulated rejection fraction, its approximate Monte Carlo standard error is:

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{MCSE}=\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/B}.
(\#eq:mcse)
\end{equation}

At a rejection rate of 80% and $B=5000$, MCSE is about `r round(100 * sqrt(.8 * .2 / 5000), 2)` percentage points. The tables use Wilson intervals for Monte Carlo uncertainty. These intervals remain informative even when a simulation observes no rejections or all rejections. Increasing $B$ does not resolve uncertainty about the real treatment effect.

# Calculate a sample size {#calculations .core-heading}



::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Calculate approximate sample sizes for two independent proportions or means.
- Explain how the target difference, variability, Type I error rate and target power affect the calculation.
- Distinguish per-group from total counts.
:::

You can now apply these ideas to two-arm treatment comparisons. The formulas below assume two independent groups with equal allocation and a two-sided test. Later, [Recruitment, precision and feasibility](#feasibility) extends planning to estimation and single-proportion examples, and [Where does my study fit?](#study-designs) considers other designs.

Having specified the chronic pain target difference and acceptable error risks, you can calculate the required number of analyzable patients. The first calculation concerns that trial; the next concerns a continuous-outcome comparison.

## How error rates and power affect sample size {.core-heading}

For familiar normal approximations, define:

\begin{equation}
f(\alpha,\beta)=\left(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta}\right)^2.
(\#eq:multiplier)
\end{equation}

Here $z_q$ is a standard-normal quantile. These formulas make the relationships visible; the required method ultimately depends on the planned analysis [@kirkwood2003; @wang2020].

In the equations, $\alpha$ denotes the Type I error rate and $\beta$ the Type II error rate; target power is $1-\beta$. The multiplier gathers the two error targets into one quantity. A smaller Type I error rate makes a false rejection less frequent under the null, and a higher target power requires more information at the target difference. Both increase the multiplier and therefore the sample size when the other assumptions stay the same. You can read the table below without calculating z-scores yourself.

```{r multiplier}
alpha <- .05
target_power <- .90
f_ab <- (qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) + qnorm(target_power))^2
f_ab
```

For a Type I error rate of 5% and target power of 90%, the multiplier is `r round(f_ab, 2)`.

```{r multiplier-table, echo=FALSE}
grid <- expand.grid(alpha = c(.05, .01), power = c(.80, .90, .95))
grid$multiplier <- with(grid, (qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) + qnorm(power))^2)
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(grid, c("alpha", "power")), digits = 2,
  caption = "Normal-approximation sample-size multipliers for different Type I error rate and target-power choices.")
```

## Two proportions {.core-heading}

The event percentages in each group and the target difference between them are your starting inputs. For the chronic pain trial, the calculation assumes 60% relief with the novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment: a target difference of 30 percentage points.

For two independent groups of equal size and a two-sided test, the tutorial and apps use the normal approximation in R's `power.prop.test()` [@rcore]. You specify the two event rates, Type I error rate and target power. The result is the required analyzable number per group, before allowing for losses.

```{r proportions}
pi_t <- .60
pi_c <- .30
pain_plan <- power.prop.test(p1 = pi_t, p2 = pi_c,
  sig.level = .05, power = .90,
  alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
n_raw <- pain_plan$n
n_per_group <- ceiling(n_raw)
pain_lab_n <- n_per_group
c(per_group = n_per_group, total = 2 * n_per_group)
```

```{r proportions-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=n_per_group, `Analyzable total`=2*n_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Analyzable sample size for the chronic-pain trial using the normal planning approximation.")
```

The unrounded result is `r round(n_raw, 2)` patients per group. Rounding upward gives `r n_per_group` per group, or `r 2 * n_per_group` in total. This is the count used in the recruitment and fixed-sample sensitivity examples below. The `strict = TRUE` setting counts significant results in either direction for the two-sided test.

The calculation targets 90% power under the stated assumptions. Actual power for the planned test can differ because the calculation is approximate; simulation lets you examine that performance. Your report should identify the method, assumptions and rounding, and account for expected losses separately.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-definitive-sample">
<summary>Common misconception: the calculator provides one definitive minimum number</summary>

The calculated sample size depends on the effect, event rates or variability, error targets and analysis method you specify. It is a conditional planning result. Check plausible alternative assumptions and whether the reported number is per group or for the whole study before interpreting it.

</details>

```{r proportion-changes}
proportion_cases <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("Original", "Smaller difference", "Lower probabilities",
               "Type I error rate 1%", "Power 95%"),
  treatment = c(.60, .60, .30, .60, .60),
  control = c(.30, .45, .15, .30, .30),
  alpha = c(.05, .05, .05, .01, .05),
  power = c(.90, .90, .90, .90, .95))
proportion_cases$per_group <- mapply(sample_size_two_proportions,
  proportion_cases$treatment, proportion_cases$control,
  proportion_cases$alpha, proportion_cases$power)
proportion_cases$total <- 2 * proportion_cases$per_group
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(proportion_cases,
  c("treatment", "control", "alpha", "power")),
  caption = "Analyzable sample sizes under alternative binary-outcome assumptions, using the same normal planning approximation as the tutorial and apps.")
```

You can compare each row with the original. Halving the difference does not necessarily multiply binary sample size by exactly four: changing a probability also changes its variance. In the lower-probabilities row, treatment relief remains twice the control probability.

Read a row as a conditional statement: if those event probabilities and that analysis are reasonable, then this is the approximate number required for the specified error targets. The row is not evidence that the intervention will achieve that benefit. The smaller-difference row needs more participants because sampling variation makes that difference harder to distinguish from zero.

### Preventing gestational diabetes {#adherence .core-heading}

Suppose you want to find out whether probiotic supplementation prevents gestational diabetes in pregnant women with overweight or obesity (BMI at least 25 kg/m²). Randomly allocate women to probiotics or no probiotics, with otherwise comparable care, and assess gestational diabetes using a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Specify the supplement, diagnostic criteria and assessment time before planning. An assessment at 20–24 weeks needs justification against applicable clinical guidance: NICE generally recommends risk-based testing at 24–28 weeks [@nicegdm]. If supplementation is observed rather than randomized, confounding needs a different analysis and planning method.

For this calculation only, assume gestational diabetes occurs in 20% without probiotics and is expected in 8% with probiotics: an expected reduction of 12 percentage points. Choose a target reduction of 10 points, corresponding to 20% versus 10%, and a clinical threshold of 5 points. All these values are hypothetical teaching assumptions.

The [lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=adherence) treats a positive difference as beneficial. Therefore enter remaining free of gestational diabetes as the favorable event: 80% without probiotics and 90% with probiotics. Its 10-point increase is exactly the same absolute difference as the 10-point reduction in disease. Record which event you entered and its direction; the clinical question remains prevention of gestational diabetes.

```{r adherence-case}
adherence_case <- teaching_case("adherence")
adherence_plan <- teaching_case_spec("adherence")
adherence_plan$n <- plan_n(adherence_plan, "testing",
  adherence_case$inputs$target_power)
c(analyzable_per_group = adherence_plan$n,
  recruit_per_group = adjust_for_dropout(adherence_plan$n,
    adherence_case$inputs$dropout),
  planning_power = spec_power(adherence_plan))
```

```{r adherence-case-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=adherence_plan$n, `Recruit per group`=adjust_for_dropout(adherence_plan$n,adherence_case$inputs$dropout), `Planning power`=percent(spec_power(adherence_plan)),check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Sample size and recruitment requirements for the hypothetical gestational-diabetes prevention trial.")
```

[Activity: Gestational-diabetes prevention trial](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=adherence). Compare recruitment with a limit of 240 women and 15% expected loss per arm. Then hold the planned sample fixed and reduce the percentage remaining free of gestational diabetes with probiotics from 90% to 85%, while keeping the comparison at 80%. This corresponds to a smaller disease reduction, from 20% to 15%. Explain why power changes while the original recruitment plan and clinical threshold remain fixed.

Under these assumptions, the required recruitment total is `r 2 * adjust_for_dropout(adherence_plan$n, adherence_case$inputs$dropout)`, exceeding the proposed limit of 240. This is a reason to reconsider recruitment, collaboration or the study's aim. Increasing the assumed benefit merely to obtain a smaller n would not supply the missing evidence.

## Two means {.core-heading}

For a continuous outcome, you should identify the target difference and the standard deviation in the same measurement units before calculating.

For a mean difference $\delta$ and common population standard deviation $\sigma$:

\begin{equation}
n\approx f(\alpha,\beta)\frac{2\sigma^2}{\delta^2}.
(\#eq:means)
\end{equation}

Suppose comparable evidence suggests a 4-unit expected difference in a normally distributed improvement score. Use a more conservative 3-unit target difference, with SD 5 in both groups, while patients and clinicians judge a 2-unit benefit clinically important. This is a hypothetical score, not a bounded clinical scale. Keep Type I error rate at 5% and power at 90%.

```{r means}
delta <- 3
sigma <- 5
n_per_group <- ceiling(f_ab * 2 * sigma^2 / delta^2)
c(per_group = n_per_group, total = 2 * n_per_group)
```

```{r means-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=n_per_group, `Analyzable total`=2*n_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Approximate analyzable sample size for the continuous-outcome comparison.")
```

The equal-allocation total is `r 2 * n_per_group`, rather than rounding the unrounded total to 117. The t-test calculation accounts for estimating variance:

```{r t-test-planning}
t_plan <- power.t.test(delta = 3, sd = 5, sig.level = .05,
  power = .90, type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided",
  strict = TRUE)
t_plan
c(per_group = ceiling(t_plan$n), total = 2 * ceiling(t_plan$n))
```

```{r t-test-planning-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Method=c("Normal approximation", "Planned two-sample t test"), `Analyzable per group`=c(n_per_group,ceiling(t_plan$n)), `Analyzable total`=2*c(n_per_group,ceiling(t_plan$n)), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Sample size requirements under two planning methods.")
```

These results distinguish a transparent normal approximation from a calculation for the planned t test. A small difference in n comes from the method, rather than from a different clinical question. Report the method used and round within each group before doubling; recruitment losses are considered separately.

Return to your study plan: record the input values, software or formula, sidedness, allocation and rounded counts. The mean calculation here assumes a common variance and plans a pooled two-sample t test. R's default `t.test()` uses Welch's unequal-variance method; choosing that analysis needs matching planning assumptions. Similarly, continuity corrections or exact methods can change binary results. Matching methods matters more than forcing two calculators to display the same number [@rcore; @julious2023].

```{r mean-changes}
mean_cases <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("Original", "Half the difference", "Twice the SD",
               "Type I error rate 1%", "Power 95%"),
  difference = c(3, 1.5, 3, 3, 3), sd = c(5, 5, 10, 5, 5),
  alpha = c(.05, .05, .05, .01, .05),
  power = c(.90, .90, .90, .90, .95))
mean_cases$per_group <- mapply(sample_size_two_means,
  mean_cases$difference, mean_cases$sd, mean_cases$alpha, mean_cases$power)
mean_cases$total <- 2 * mean_cases$per_group
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(mean_cases, c("alpha", "power")),
  caption = "Analyzable sample sizes under alternative mean differences, variability and error targets, using the simple normal approximation.")
```

Before rounding, halving the difference or doubling the SD multiplies the required sample size by four. Explain this using equation \@ref(eq:means).

### A rehabilitation case {#rehabilitation .core-heading}

The same calculation could compare two rehabilitation programs, rather than two drugs. Suppose the primary outcome is improvement at six weeks on a hypothetical continuous mobility score. The expected difference is 4 units, the target difference is 3 units, and patients and clinicians judge a 2-unit benefit clinically meaningful. Use a common SD of 5 units. For this illustration, independent patients are randomized to the two programs and the improvement scores are approximately normal.

```{r rehabilitation-case}
rehabilitation_case <- teaching_case("rehabilitation")
rehabilitation_plan <- teaching_case_spec("rehabilitation")
rehabilitation_plan$n <- plan_n(rehabilitation_plan, "testing",
  rehabilitation_case$inputs$target_power)
c(analyzable_per_group = rehabilitation_plan$n,
  total = 2 * rehabilitation_plan$n,
  recruitment_total = 2 * adjust_for_dropout(rehabilitation_plan$n,
    rehabilitation_case$inputs$dropout))
```

```{r rehabilitation-case-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=rehabilitation_plan$n, `Analyzable total`=2*rehabilitation_plan$n, `Recruit total`=2*adjust_for_dropout(rehabilitation_plan$n, rehabilitation_case$inputs$dropout), check.names=FALSE), caption="Sample size and recruitment requirements for the rehabilitation comparison.")
```

[Activity: Rehabilitation: compare two means](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=rehabilitation). Ask whether 10% expected loss and a recruitment limit of 200 make this plan feasible. Compare the confidence interval with the 2-unit clinical threshold. Although an improvement score uses before/after information within each patient, this example analyses one score per patient across two independent groups. A single-group paired comparison, repeated-measures model, or baseline-adjusted analysis needs its own planning method.

The expected-loss adjustment gives a recruitment total of `r 2 * adjust_for_dropout(rehabilitation_plan$n, rehabilitation_case$inputs$dropout)`, below this example's cap of 200. Meeting the cap and power target still leaves questions about the credibility of the assumptions, measurement quality and the precision needed for a clinical decision.

<div class="core-next">Continue along the core route: <a href="#account-for-expected-losses">Recruitment and expected losses</a>.</div>

# Read power curves {#curves .advanced-heading}



::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Read power curves.
- Compare plausible effects and sample sizes.
- Assess sensitivity and recruitment limits while keeping the planned sample size fixed when appropriate.
:::

The chronic pain calculation uses one set of assumptions. What if the true benefit is smaller, or recruitment limits the number of patients? Power curves show how the answer changes.

## Activity: Chronic pain: explore power and recruitment {#activity-2-can-the-feasible-study-answer-the-question .advanced-heading}

A single calculation hides its dependence on uncertain inputs. Chapter 11 of @superpowerbook2022 motivates examining power across a range of sample sizes and effects. Here you keep the chronic pain plan fixed and examine true control relief of 30% with treatment relief of 45%, 50% or 60%. The case still has an expected difference of 40 percentage points, a target difference of 30 points and a clinical threshold of 20 points; these curves explore performance if reality differs from the expectation.

Suppose the clinic can recruit 200 patients in total, with 10% expected loss in each arm. This corresponds to 100 recruited and an expected 90 analyzable patients per group. That expected count is not guaranteed.

```{r curve-settings}
curve_spec <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = 90,
  p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
  width_target = .20)
effect_sizes <- c(.15, .20, .30)
target_power <- .90
recruitment_cap <- 200
expected_loss <- .10
analyzable_cap <- floor(recruitment_cap / 2 * (1 - expected_loss))
```

```{r power-curves, fig.cap="Power for treatment differences of 15, 20 and 30 percentage points. Dashed lines show 90% target power and the recruitment limit of 90 analyzable patients per group.", fig.alt="Three curves show that smaller treatment benefits need more patients. A horizontal line marks 90 percent power and a vertical line marks 90 analyzable patients per group."}
curve_table <- power_curve_data(curve_spec, effect_sizes, seq(5, 200, 5))
plot_power_curves(curve_table, target_power, analyzable_cap)
```

```{r cap-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cap_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(effect_sizes, function(effect) {
  x <- curve_spec; x$p_treatment <- x$p_control + effect
  data.frame(absolute_benefit = effect,
    analyzable_per_group = analyzable_cap,
    approximate_power_at_cap = spec_power(x, analyzable_cap),
    per_group_for_target = plan_n(x, target_power = target_power))
}))
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(cap_results, "approximate_power_at_cap",
  points = "absolute_benefit"),
  format = if (knitr::is_html_output()) "html" else "latex",
  col.names = c("True difference (percentage points)", "Analyzable patients per group",
    "Power with 90 per group", "Patients per group for 90% power"),
  caption = "Power with 90 patients per group and sample size needed for 90% power.")
```

## Hold sample size fixed and vary the effect {.advanced-heading}

Figure \@ref(fig:effect-curve) answers a different question: with 90 analyzable patients per group, how does power change across possible treatment benefits? The target-power crossing describes a detectable effect at that target.

```{r effect-curve, fig.cap="Approximate power across true treatment benefits with 90 analyzable patients per group and 30% control relief. The horizontal reference marks 90% power.", fig.alt="Power rises with the assumed positive treatment benefit; the horizontal reference is 90 percent power."}
effect_grid <- seq(0, .40, .005)
effect_power <- vapply(effect_grid, function(effect) {
  x <- curve_spec; x$p_treatment <- x$p_control + effect
  spec_power(x)
}, numeric(1))
plot(effect_grid * 100, effect_power, type = "l", lwd = 2,
  col = "#176675", ylim = c(0, 1), yaxt = "n",
  xlab = "Absolute treatment benefit (percentage points)", ylab = "Power (%)")
axis(2, at = seq(0, 1, .2), labels = paste0(seq(0, 100, 20), "%"))
abline(h = target_power, lty = 2)
```

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-detection-boundary">
<summary>Common misconception: the target-power crossing is a detection boundary</summary>

An effect below the target-power crossing can still produce a significant result; an effect above it can still go undetected. The curve describes probabilities across repeated studies, not a boundary separating detectable from undetectable effects. The clinical threshold is a separate judgment.

</details>

::: {.activity}
Predict. Which effect assumption is most demanding at the same power target?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-curves-predict">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The 15-percentage-point difference requires the largest sample for the same power target, followed by 20 points and then 30 points. With control relief fixed at 30% and the analysis and error targets unchanged, smaller differences are harder to distinguish from sampling variation. This comparison concerns true treatment differences; changing the clinical threshold alone does not change the power of a test of zero difference.

</details>

Explore. [Activity: Chronic pain: explore power and recruitment](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_curves). In the [lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_curves) set a fixed sample of 90 per group, control 30%, and treatment 60%. Compare true treatment relief of 50% and 45% while keeping the expected difference, target difference and clinical threshold distinct. Use the prepared curves above to view all three scenarios together.

Explain. Which assumptions make the target feasible? How do you distinguish 200 recruited patients from 180 expected analyzable patients?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-curve-assumptions">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The displayed plan reaches 90% power at the 30-point target difference with 90 analyzable patients per group, given 30% standard-treatment relief, the chosen test and a 5% Type I error rate. It does not reach that power target for the smaller 20-point clinical threshold or the 15-point alternative. The recruitment limit is 200 people; applying 10% expected loss gives 180 expected analyzable outcomes, or 90 per group. Feasibility therefore depends on the treatment difference and event rates being credible, the analysis being appropriate and retention being close to its assumption. These are expectations, rather than guaranteed counts or outcomes.

</details>


Justify. Write three sentences describing what the clinic's recruitment limit could establish. Do not increase the assumed benefit merely to make the design affordable.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-curves-justify">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Recruiting 200 patients with 10% expected loss gives an expected 180 analyzable patients, or 90 per group, rather than 200 usable outcomes. At that count, approximate power is `r percent(cap_results$approximate_power_at_cap[3])` for a true 30-point difference and `r percent(cap_results$approximate_power_at_cap[2])` for a true 20-point difference, so the plan meets the 90% target at 30 points but not at the smaller clinical threshold. Your recommendation should acknowledge that limitation and the uncertainty in retention, and consider more recruitment or a revised objective if high power at 20 points is essential, rather than choosing an unsupported larger difference.

</details>
:::

## Sensitivity is not observed post hoc power {.advanced-heading}

These curves specify hypothetical effects before interpreting a realized study.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-observed-power">
<summary>Common misconception: power calculated from the observed effect explains the completed study</summary>

Substituting the study's observed effect into a power calculation adds no useful evidence about that same result. Interpret the estimate, confidence interval, study design and limitations instead. At a fixed sample size, power across independently justified hypothetical differences can still help describe the design's capabilities [@consortee2025; @lakens2022].

</details>

For example, suppose a completed study estimates a 1-unit improvement with a 95% confidence interval from -1 to 3, while a 2-unit benefit would matter clinically. The interval includes some harm, zero, a small benefit and a clinically important benefit. The study leaves those possibilities unresolved; calculating low power from the observed 1-unit estimate does not decide between them.

With an existing records dataset, explain why that sample is available, assess data quality and missingness, and report what its estimate and interval support. A sensitivity analysis at independently justified effects can still describe a fixed design's performance. It should not use the observed effect to create additional evidence for the same study. This distinction follows the sample size justification approach in @lakens2022; [the FAQ](#common-mistakes) gives a short retrospective-study example.

# Build a simulated clinical trial {#simulation .advanced-heading}



::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Generate and analyze one hypothetical trial.
- Repeat the trial to assess rejection and interval coverage.
- Explain how Monte Carlo uncertainty differs from uncertainty in the planning assumptions.
:::

This chapter returns to the two-arm chronic pain trial and its planned analysis.

The curves in Figure \@ref(fig:power-curves) describe the performance of the chronic pain design across repeated studies. Now generate individual trials under the same assumptions to see why their estimates, intervals and decisions vary.

Simulation is especially useful when the planned analysis or dependency between observations makes a simple formula inadequate. First define the quantity to estimate, justify the data-generating assumptions, and specify the analysis. Then generate, analyze and repeat, summarize performance with Monte Carlo uncertainty, and vary uncertain assumptions [@pargent2024]. For complex models, also record failed fits and check performance under a null scenario. A simulation is only as informative as its assumptions and implementation.

## Activity: Simulate repeated chronic pain trials {#activity-3-generate-analyze-repeat-summarize .advanced-heading}

The custom-simulation approach in chapter 15 of @superpowerbook2022 starts from the planned trial and its analysis. The binary example uses the same score test as the [existing reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_simulation). This is an adaptation of the workflow, not a reproduction of the book's logistic-regression example.

[Activity: Simulate repeated chronic pain trials](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_simulation) to connect these four steps with one study and repeated studies in the app. The prepared batch and app use the same seed, sample size and analysis.

### Step 1: generate one trial {.advanced-heading}

Generate 60 independent patients per group, with relief probabilities of 30% and 60%. The simulation evaluates the 30-percentage-point target difference; the expected difference is 40 points and the clinical threshold is 20 points. Each patient's outcome is zero or one. Setting the seed makes this example reproducible.

```{r generate-trial}
set.seed(20260921)
n <- 60
control <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = .30)
treatment <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = .60)
c(control_relief = sum(control), treatment_relief = sum(treatment))
```

```{r generate-trial-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Group=c("Standard treatment", "Novel treatment"), Patients=n, `Reporting relief`=c(sum(control),sum(treatment)), `Relief percentage`=percent(c(mean(control),mean(treatment))), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Observed pain relief in one simulated trial.")
```

### Step 2: apply the planned analysis {.advanced-heading}

Use a two-sided pooled score test without continuity correction. The helper also calculates a Newcombe-Wilson interval for the risk difference [@newcombe1998]. These are different procedures: test rejection and interval exclusion of zero can occasionally disagree.

```{r analyze-trial}
one_result <- analyse_binary(sum(treatment), sum(control), n, alpha = .05)
one_result
```

```{r analyze-trial-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Measure=c("Observed treatment difference", "95% confidence interval", "p-value", "Testing decision"), Result=c(paste(round(100*one_result$estimate,1),"percentage points"), paste(round(100*one_result$lower,1),"to",round(100*one_result$upper,1),"percentage points"), formatC(one_result$p_value,format="f",digits=3), if(one_result$p_value < .05) "Reject the zero-difference null" else "Do not reject the zero-difference null")),
  caption = "Estimated benefit and testing decision in one simulated trial.")
```

`estimate` is treatment minus control; `lower` and `upper` are confidence limits. The p-value tests a zero difference. The helper's score-test p-value can be checked against R:

```{r independent-check}
reference <- prop.test(c(sum(treatment), sum(control)), c(n, n),
  correct = FALSE)
c(helper_p = one_result$p_value, R_p = reference$p.value)
```

```{r independent-check-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Method=c("Tutorial helper", "R score test"), `p-value`=formatC(c(one_result$p_value,reference$p.value),format="f",digits=4), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Agreement between two implementations of the planned score test.")
```

This comparison checks the p-value, not the interval: `prop.test()` uses a different interval calculation. When both groups have all successes or all failures, the helper explicitly returns a p-value of one rather than an undefined statistic.

### Step 3: repeat independent trials {.advanced-heading}

The efficient helper generates binomial counts instead of storing every patient's record. This is equivalent to adding up independent binary outcomes in each group. It applies the same analysis to every trial, using a seed set once before the batch.

```{r repeat-trials}
trial_spec <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = 60,
  p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, alpha = .05,
  threshold = .20, width_target = .30, B = 5000, seed = 20260921)
trials <- simulate_trials(trial_spec)
head(trials$results, 4)
```

### Step 4: summarize what the design achieves {.advanced-heading}

```{r trial-summary}
knitr::kable(display_simulation_summary(simulation_summary(trials)),
  caption = "Repeated-trial operating characteristics, with Monte Carlo standard errors and 95% intervals.")
```

The rejection rate estimates power at these probabilities. Coverage is the percentage of confidence intervals containing the generating difference. The width-target rate is the percentage with a full interval width no greater than 30 percentage points. These are three separate properties.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-simulation-repetitions">
<summary>Common misconception: running more simulations makes the study more powerful</summary>

Increasing the number of simulated studies makes the estimated rejection rate more precise. It does not add patients to each study or increase its underlying power. Increasing the patients per group changes the study; increasing the simulation repetitions improves your numerical description of it.

</details>

```{r trial-intervals, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Risk-difference confidence intervals from the first 30 simulated trials. Filled dots indicate rejection of zero. Reference lines mark the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold and the 30-percentage-point generating effect used for planning.", fig.alt="Intervals vary from trial to trial. Separate lines mark zero, the 20-point clinical threshold and the 30-point generating effect. The preceding table reports rejection, coverage and attainment of the full interval width target across all 5,000 trials."}
plot_trial_intervals(trials$results, trial_spec)
```

## Compare simulation with a planning approximation {.advanced-heading}

```{r simulation-benchmark}
c(simulated_power = mean(trials$results$reject),
  approximate_planning_power = spec_power(trial_spec))
```

```{r simulation-benchmark-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Method=c("Repeated-trial simulation", "Planning approximation"), Power=percent(c(mean(trials$results$reject),spec_power(trial_spec)))),
  caption = "Power estimated by simulation and by the planning approximation.")
```

A difference can reflect [Monte Carlo error](#monte-carlo-error) or the approximation used for binary planning. Increasing the number of simulations reduces only the Monte Carlo component. Simulation is a way to investigate the analysis under explicit assumptions, not an automatic guarantee that those assumptions fit a real study.

::: {.activity}
Predict. Keep 60 patients per group. What happens if true treatment relief is 45% rather than 60%?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-simulation-predict">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

With control relief still at 30%, the true treatment difference falls from 30 to 15 percentage points. Across repeated trials with 60 patients per group, observed differences should center around 15 points and fewer trials should reject the null hypothesis. The original sample size and the 20-point clinical threshold stay fixed; the true 15-point benefit is below that threshold. Individual trials can still produce significant results, which would not by itself establish a clinically worthwhile benefit.

</details>

Explore. In the [lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_simulation) retain the planning probabilities, choose *Custom effect or variability*, set generating control to 30% and treatment to 45%, then run many studies. The planned sample must stay fixed. Repeat under no true effect.

Explain. Report the generating probabilities, patients per group, replications, rejection rate and its Monte Carlo interval. Distinguish uncertainty in the simulation from uncertainty in the clinical assumptions.

```{r model-smaller-trial, include=FALSE}
model_changed_trial_spec <- trial_spec
model_changed_trial_spec$p_treatment <- .45
model_changed_simulation <- simulation_summary(simulate_trials(model_changed_trial_spec))[1, ]
```


<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-simulation-report">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

For the smaller-effect scenario, the generating probabilities are 30% standard-treatment relief and 45% novel-treatment relief, with 60 patients per group and 5,000 independent simulated trials. Using the prepared seed and analysis, the rejection rate is `r percent(model_changed_simulation$estimate)`, with a 95% Monte Carlo interval of `r percent(model_changed_simulation$MC_lower_95)` to `r percent(model_changed_simulation$MC_upper_95)`. This estimates the probability of rejecting zero under that specified 15-point true difference. The Monte Carlo interval describes uncertainty from a finite simulation batch, rather than uncertainty about whether these population rates are realistic or the treatment-effect interval from one trial. A different seed may give a slightly different simulation estimate.

</details>


Justify. Would the original plan still answer the clinical question? State what extra evidence or design change would help.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-simulation-justify">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The original plan evaluates power at a true 30-point difference. If the true difference is only 15 points, the trial has lower power to reject zero and its true benefit falls below the 20-point clinical threshold. It can still estimate the difference, but it may give an inconclusive result and a significant result would not establish that the clinical threshold has been exceeded. Better evidence on treatment response, control response and clinical importance would help assess whether the planning assumptions remain credible. A larger sample or collaboration could improve precision or power for an independently justified difference; adding simulation repetitions would only improve the numerical precision of the simulation estimate.

</details>
:::

# Recruitment, precision and feasibility {#feasibility .core-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Adjust recruitment for expected losses.
- Interpret confidence intervals against zero and a clinical threshold.
- Plan useful precision for a prevalence estimate or pilot feasibility outcome.
- Assess what an existing dataset can establish for a new research question.
- Explain planning options when a rare disease limits recruitment.
:::

The chronic pain trial needs enough analyzable outcomes, but recruitment is only part of its plan. You should also allow for losses and consider whether the resulting estimates would guide a clinical decision.

The core route follows recruitment, clinical interpretation, sensitivity and feasibility.
