The advanced sections ask what changes when useful precision, an existing dataset or a feasibility decision becomes the main planning goal. They extend the same question-to-analysis reasoning rather than introduce unrelated calculations.

## Account for expected losses {.core-heading}



If $n$ analyzable patients are needed in each arm and the expected dropout proportion is $r$, the simple inflation is:

\begin{equation}
n_{\mathrm{recruit,arm}}=\left\lceil\frac{n}{1-r}\right\rceil.
(\#eq:dropout)
\end{equation}

```{r recruitment}
analyzable_per_group <- pain_lab_n
recruit_per_group <- ceiling(analyzable_per_group / (1 - .05))
c(analyzable_per_group = analyzable_per_group,
  recruit_per_group = recruit_per_group, recruit_total = 2 * recruit_per_group)
```

```{r recruitment-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=analyzable_per_group, `Recruit per group`=recruit_per_group, `Recruit total`=2*recruit_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Chronic-pain recruitment target allowing for 5% expected loss.")
```

The simulations here condition on analyzable counts and do not model dropout.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-dropout">
<summary>Common misconception: adding the expected dropout percentage solves missing data</summary>

To allow for 10% expected loss, divide the required analyzable count by 0.90 rather than simply adding 10%. This protects the expected participant count, but does not guarantee it. Recruiting extra participants also does not remove bias caused by missing outcomes or treatment non-adherence.

</details>

## Interpret a confidence interval clinically {.core-heading}



For the continuous improvement-score case, the expected difference is 4 units, the target difference is 3 units and the clinical threshold is 2 units. Compare three hypothetical 95% confidence intervals:

| Interval | Interpretation |
|:--|:--|
| 0.2 to 2.8 | Zero is excluded, but both small and clinically important benefits remain compatible. |
| -0.8 to 3.2 | Some harm, no effect and clinically important benefit remain compatible. |
| 2.2 to 4.2 | The interval lies above the specified clinical threshold. |

Table: (\#tab:clinical-intervals) Interpreting hypothetical 95% intervals against zero and a 2-unit clinical threshold.

A confidence procedure with 95% coverage contains the fixed population effect in about 95% of repetitions under its assumptions. It does not assign a 95% probability to the fixed truth after observing one interval. Precision and clinical interpretation complement the power calculation [@sandoval2025].

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-power-precision">
<summary>Common misconception: high power guarantees clinically useful precision</summary>

A study can detect a difference from zero while leaving considerable uncertainty about whether the benefit is clinically worthwhile. Power concerns the testing decision; precision concerns the interval's width. Consider both when deciding whether the study can answer the clinical question.

</details>

<div class="core-next">Continue along the core route: <a href="#stress-test-the-study-plan">Sensitivity analysis and feasibility</a>.</div>

## Plan for precision {.advanced-heading}



The [lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=mean_precision) offers *Estimate with a target interval width* alongside testing and fixed-resource goals. Specify the full width, in the outcome's original units. For the continuous improvement score, keep the expected difference at 4 units, target difference at 3 units and clinical threshold at 2 units. Use SD 5 and a target full width of 4 units:

```{r precision-plan}
precision_spec <- study_spec(outcome = "means", delta = 3, sd = 5,
  threshold = 2, width_target = 4, B = 5000, seed = 20260922)
precision_spec$n <- plan_n(precision_spec, goal = "precision")
c(per_group = precision_spec$n,
  expected_full_width = anticipated_width(precision_spec),
  power_at_planning_effect = spec_power(precision_spec))
precision_batch <- simulate_trials(precision_spec)
knitr::kable(display_simulation_summary(simulation_summary(precision_batch)),
  caption = "Precision planning and realized interval performance are different quantities.")
```

```{r precision-plan-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=precision_spec$n, `Anticipated full interval width`=round(anticipated_width(precision_spec),2), `Power at the target difference`=percent(spec_power(precision_spec)),check.names=FALSE), caption="Sample size, anticipated precision and power for the improvement-score comparison.")
```

For normal data, the curve gives expected full t-interval width. For binary data, it uses a plug-in Newcombe-Wilson width at the assumed probabilities, not exact expected width. Neither criterion guarantees that each realized interval will meet the target; the simulation reports the fraction that does so separately [@sandoval2025; @newcombe1998].

::: {.activity}
Compare goals. [Activity: Plan the precision of a mean difference](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=mean_precision). In the [lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=mean_precision) choose *Continuous outcome*, expected difference 4, target difference 3, SD 5, clinical threshold 2, Type I error rate 5% and full width 4. The outcome here is an improvement score. Compare the sample selected for estimation with the sample selected for 80% power. Explain why the same research question might require considering both criteria.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-precision-versus-power">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

With SD 5 and the same two-group analysis, the expected full-width target of 4 units requires `r precision_spec$n` analyzable patients per group; the 80% power target at a 3-unit difference requires `r plan_n(precision_spec, goal = "testing", target_power = .80)` per group. Precision planning concerns how accurately the difference can be estimated; power planning concerns how often the test rejects zero at the specified true difference. Your study question may require both a useful interval width and an adequate chance of detecting a worthwhile effect. If both are requirements, the plan should satisfy both under justified assumptions. An expected interval-width target does not guarantee that every realized interval meets it.

</details>

:::

## Estimate one proportion: a prevalence survey {#prevalence .advanced-heading}



Here the design changes from a two-arm treatment comparison to a survey estimating one population proportion. There is no treatment or control arm; sample size is chosen for a useful margin of error.

For example, before another pain study, a service may need to know how common a symptom is among its eligible patients. Similar estimation questions arise when planning recruitment or retention in a feasibility study. The question is how accurately to estimate a percentage, rather than how often to reject a zero treatment difference [@pourhoseingholi2013; @ying2025].

Suppose a service wants to estimate the percentage of eligible patients reporting a symptom. It wants a 95% confidence interval with an approximate margin of error of 5 percentage points: half-width $d=0.05$, or a full width of 10 percentage points. This is a simple independent-sample prevalence example, with one total sample rather than n per treatment arm.

For an anticipated population proportion $p_0$, the familiar normal approximation gives:

\begin{equation}
n\approx\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}^{2}p_0(1-p_0)}{d^2}.
(\#eq:single-proportion)
\end{equation}

Here $p_0$ is an assumption used before data collection, not an observed sample result. If comparable evidence suggests a prevalence of 20% ($p_0=0.20$), the approximate requirement is 246 completed observations. If there is no useful prior estimate, 50% ($p_0=0.50$) gives the largest value of $p_0(1-p_0)$ and an approximate requirement of 385.

```{r single-proportion-precision}
prevalence_known <- proportion_precision_plan(p = .20,
  full_width = .10, confidence = .95)
prevalence_unknown <- proportion_precision_plan(p = .20,
  full_width = .10, confidence = .95, unknown_p = TRUE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  scenario = c("Prior estimate 20%", "Unknown: use 50% for planning"),
  planning_percentage = percent(c(prevalence_known$planning_p,
    prevalence_unknown$planning_p)),
  completed_observations = c(prevalence_known$n, prevalence_unknown$n)),
  caption = "Approximate prevalence sample sizes for a 95% interval with a 5-percentage-point margin of error.")
```

The conservative 50% choice concerns absolute precision for one proportion under this approximation. It is not a general substitute for unknown control and treatment percentages in a power calculation. For a rare outcome, an absolute margin of five percentage points might be unhelpfully wide; event counts and the chosen interval method also matter.

[Activity: Estimate a percentage with useful precision](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=prevalence). Compare margins of error of 5 and 2.5 percentage points. The latter requires about four times as many completed observations under the formula. The app shows a Wilson interval for an illustrative realized sample; its width can differ from the planning approximation. No formula here guarantees that every realized interval meets the target. Representative recruitment matters as well: a larger convenience sample does not automatically remove selection bias [@whitley2002; @wang2020].

## Reuse an existing dataset for a different question {#dataset-reuse .advanced-heading}



A bachelor project may start with an existing dataset rather than new recruitment. Suppose a completed chronic pain trial included 200 patients and also recorded sleep difficulty before treatment. Your new question is: what percentage of these trial participants reported sleep difficulty at baseline? This differs from the trial's original question about treatment effectiveness.

Baseline sleep information is available for 180 participants; 72 reported difficulty. The observed percentage is 72/180 = 40%. The sample size is already fixed, so assess the precision the available data provide instead of calculating how many patients to recruit.

```{r reused-dataset}
sleep_result <- single_proportion_interval(events = 72, n = 180,
  confidence = .95)
sleep_result
```

```{r reused-dataset-summary, echo=FALSE}
sleep_limits <- wilson_interval(.40, 180)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Measure = c("Patients in the dataset", "With baseline sleep information",
    "Reporting sleep difficulty", "Observed percentage", "95% Wilson confidence interval"),
  Result = c("200", "180", "72", "40.0%",
    paste(percent(sleep_limits[1, 1]), "to", percent(sleep_limits[1, 2])))),
  caption = "A new descriptive question answered using an existing chronic-pain trial dataset.")
```

The interval describes sampling uncertainty under the model. It does not account for possible differences between the 20 patients with missing information and those who answered. The trial's eligibility criteria also restrict whom these results describe: its participants may not represent all patients with chronic pain. Random allocation supports the original treatment comparison; it does not make this baseline sample representative of a broader population.

The original trial's power calculation does not transfer to this new question. Check that the required variables and time points are available, that reuse is permitted, and that the analysis fits the new objective. For a new association question, you would also need to consider confounding and the relevant model. Avoid calculating observed post hoc power; report the estimate, interval and limitations [@lakens2022; @consortee2025].

Before examining the new results, document why the sample is fixed and what precision would be useful. The number available is a resource constraint, not evidence of adequate information. For a comparison, evaluate independently justified differences at that fixed sample size; for this descriptive question, examine the attainable interval width. If it is too wide for the intended decision, narrow the claim or explain that more data would be needed. Exploring an existing dataset can generate hypotheses, but should not be presented as a prospectively planned confirmation.

::: {.activity}
Adapt the question. Identify the new outcome, target population, available sample and missing observations. Would an interval of this width answer your project question? Record these decisions in the [Activity: Record and justify your assumptions](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=assumptions_report), using a fixed-resource estimation goal.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-existing-data">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The new outcome is baseline sleep difficulty, and the population directly described is the eligible chronic pain trial population, rather than all people with chronic pain. The dataset contains 200 patients, with sleep information for 180 and missing information for 20. Among those with information, 72/180 = 40% reported difficulty; the 95% Wilson interval is `r percent(sleep_limits[1, 1])` to `r percent(sleep_limits[1, 2])`.

Whether this precision is useful depends on a decision specified for the project. It may support a broad descriptive estimate, but would not support a requirement to estimate the percentage within 2 percentage points. The report should explain the fixed sample, missing information and restricted population. This is an estimation question, so the original treatment-effect power calculation does not establish adequacy for the new purpose.

</details>

:::

## Stress-test the study plan {.core-heading}



Return to the chronic pain plan. Sensitivity analysis answers two related questions: how many patients would be needed under different assumptions, and how would the original sample perform if those assumptions were wrong? First compare the required counts at the clinical threshold, target difference and expected difference. Then hold the original planned sample fixed. In the [lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_curves), change *Reality may differ from the plan* for this second question [@cook2018delta2; @lakens2022].

```{r pain-target-sensitivity, echo=FALSE}
pain_target_n <- ceiling(power.prop.test(p1 = .60, p2 = .30,
  sig.level = .05, power = .90, alternative = "two.sided",
  strict = TRUE)$n)
pain_alternatives <- c(.50, .60, .70)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `True novel-treatment relief` = percent(pain_alternatives),
  `Difference from 30% standard-treatment relief` = paste(c(20, 30, 40), "percentage points"),
  `Required per group for 90% power` = vapply(pain_alternatives,
    function(p) ceiling(power.prop.test(p1 = p, p2 = .30,
      sig.level = .05, power = .90, alternative = "two.sided",
      strict = TRUE)$n), numeric(1)),
  `Power at the original sample size` = percent(vapply(pain_alternatives,
    function(p) power.prop.test(n = pain_target_n, p1 = p, p2 = .30,
      sig.level = .05, alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)$power,
    numeric(1))), check.names = FALSE),
  caption = paste("Chronic-pain sensitivity: alternative required counts and approximate power with the original", pain_target_n, "patients per group held fixed."))
```

This comparison keeps standard-treatment relief at 30%, the Type I error rate at 5%, and the analysis unchanged. Record why the alternatives are plausible and which uncertainty matters most for the decision. Also vary the standard-treatment rate where relevant: the same difference at different event rates need not require the same sample. The continuous-outcome example below illustrates the corresponding role of variability.

```{r fixed-plan-sensitivity}
plan <- study_spec(outcome = "means", n = ceiling(t_plan$n), delta = 3, sd = 5)
smaller <- plan; smaller$delta <- 1
more_variable <- plan; more_variable$sd <- 7
scenarios <- list(plan, smaller, more_variable)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = c("Target difference", "Smaller true difference", "Larger standard deviation"),
  `Analyzable patients per group` = vapply(scenarios, function(x) x$n, numeric(1)),
  Power = percent(vapply(scenarios, spec_power, numeric(1))),
  `Expected full interval width (score units)` = vapply(scenarios, anticipated_width, numeric(1)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  digits = 3, caption = "Continuous-outcome sensitivity with the sample selected for 90% target power held fixed.")
```

## Underpowered studies: what if the study is too small for its purpose? {#what-if-the-study-is-too-small-for-its-purpose .core-heading}



Low power makes inconclusive results more likely under the planning alternative. Among selected statistically significant results, effects can be exaggerated. Larger samples reduce sampling variation but do not automatically remove bias.

For the chronic pain trial, a study with low power at the 30-percentage-point target difference would often fail to detect that benefit even if it were real. A non-significant result would not establish that the treatments are equally effective. Examine the estimated benefit and confidence interval against zero and the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold.

## Ways to increase power {#increase-power .core-heading}



Before collecting data, consider whether you can obtain more information about the treatment effect. Table \@ref(tab:increase-power) separates changes to the study from changes to its error targets.

For continuous outcomes, Candel and van Breukelen show how allocation, baseline information and within-person comparisons affect efficiency [@candel2023]. These gains depend on the design and analysis; their formulas cannot be transferred unchanged to binary outcomes. Prespecify useful baseline adjustment and recalculate for the intended model. A crossover design is only appropriate when treatment reversibility, disease stability and carryover permit it.

| Option | Why it can help | What to consider |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Increase the analyzable sample | More independent patients reduce sampling uncertainty at the same true effect. | Extend recruitment or collaborate across sites. Allow for expected losses and check that recruitment is feasible. |
| Improve follow-up and outcome completeness | Retaining more outcomes protects the analyzable sample. | Address reasons for missing outcomes; a larger count alone does not remove missing-data bias. |
| Improve measurement | More reliable measurement can reduce unexplained variability in a continuous outcome and improve precision. | For pain relief, use a clear, consistent definition and assessment time. A different outcome needs its own assumptions and calculation. |
| Use an appropriate, efficient design and analysis | Prespecified adjustment for informative baseline measures, or a suitable paired or repeated-measures design, can improve precision. | These methods require different planning calculations. Repeated observations from one patient are not extra independent patients. |
| Keep allocation balanced when appropriate | For the equal-variance, equal-cost comparisons illustrated here, equal group sizes make efficient use of a fixed total. | Unequal costs, variances or other design requirements can justify another allocation. Recalculate for that design. |
| Accept a higher Type I error rate | A less stringent rejection rule increases power at the specified alternative. | It also increases the risk of rejecting a true null. Justify the error rate prospectively; changing it to make a result significant is not sound planning. |
| Use a one-sided test when the scientific question warrants it | Directing the rejection region to a prespecified direction can increase power for effects in that direction. | It does not test both directions in the same way. Specify and justify it before seeing the data; a smaller required sample is not sufficient justification [@moye2002]. |

Table: (\#tab:increase-power) Options for increasing power and the assumptions or tradeoffs they require.

A larger true benefit is easier to detect, but entering a larger assumed benefit into a calculator does not make the treatment more effective. Keep the chronic pain expected difference (40 percentage points), target difference (30 points) and clinical threshold (20 points) distinct and justified. Changing the clinical threshold alone does not increase power for a test of zero difference. Likewise, running more simulations improves the precision of the estimated power; it does not increase the study's power.

::: {.activity}
Compare plans. [Activity: Chronic pain: one study and many studies](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many). Keep standard-treatment relief at 30%, novel-treatment relief at 60% and the Type I error rate at 5%. Compare 50 and 80 analyzable patients per group. Which plan detects the specified benefit more often? What would obtaining the larger sample require in practice? Record the recruitment implications in your study plan.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-larger-study-resources">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

With the same population assumptions and test, 80 analyzable patients per group should detect the 30-point difference more often than 50 per group. In the prepared simulation, the rejection percentages are `r percent(power_results$simulated_power[3])` and `r percent(power_results$simulated_power[2])`, respectively. At 10% expected loss, the corresponding recruitment targets are 89 per group (178 total) and 56 per group (112 total), after rounding within each arm. The larger design therefore needs capacity for 66 additional recruits, with implications for recruitment time, staffing, funding and participant burden. More information can reduce uncertainty, but the feasibility of obtaining it also needs justification.

</details>

:::

If none of these options makes the study informative and feasible, reconsider an overly broad aim, collaborate, or decide not to proceed with an efficacy study. For a rare disease, however, low power alone need not rule out a useful controlled study; see [What if the disease is rare?](#rare-diseases) below. A feasibility study should be judged against feasibility aims rather than treated as a miniature confirmatory trial [@lakens2022]. Changing the aim changes what the study can establish; it does not make the original treatment comparison more powerful. Broader eligibility can affect variability and generalizability. Clustered designs, nonparametric analyses and Bayesian planning require appropriate methods beyond the calculations illustrated here [@hayes1999; @happ2019; @pezeshk2003].

<div class="core-next">Continue along the core route: <a href="#write-a-sample-size-justification">Write a sample size justification</a>.</div>

## What if the disease is rare? {#rare-diseases .advanced-heading}



For a rare disease, the number of eligible patients may impose a genuine limit on recruitment. Start by documenting how many patients could realistically participate, over what period and across which centers. Then assess what that sample could establish.

This is the same feasibility problem as the chronic pain plan, with a more restrictive recruitment ceiling. The aim is a valid study with useful information, rather than finding a calculation that happens to fit the available number.

1. Establish the recruitment ceiling. Work with specialist centers, registries and patient organizations. Consider collaboration across countries, eligibility criteria and ways to reduce travel and follow-up burden. Distinguish the number of people with the disease from the number eligible and willing to participate [@fdarare2023].
2. Use knowledge of the disease's natural course. Previous studies and registries can inform progression, variability, suitable assessment times and meaningful outcomes. Check whether these data describe the population you intend to study. If this knowledge is insufficient, a natural-history study may be a useful research objective in its own right [@fdanaturalhistory2019].
3. Obtain useful information from each participant. Use reliable, clinically meaningful measurements and minimize missing outcomes. Where appropriate, retain a continuous outcome rather than reducing it to "response/no response", and prespecify adjustment for informative baseline measurements. These choices require a matching analysis and sample size method [@emasmall2006].
4. Consider another design when appropriate. Crossover or n-of-1 designs may suit stable conditions with reversible treatment effects and manageable carryover. They generally do not suit irreversible treatments or rapidly progressing disease. Prespecified adaptive or Bayesian approaches may also help, but require specialist planning; they do not guarantee that fewer patients will suffice [@emasmall2006; @fdarare2023].
5. Preserve a credible comparison. Randomization remains valuable. Registry or historical controls can sometimes help, but differences in patient severity, treatment era and outcome measurement can bias the comparison. They are not an automatic replacement for a concurrent control group [@fdaexternal2023].
6. Explain the remaining uncertainty. Evaluate attainable power across plausible effects and the anticipated confidence interval width. A small randomized study may still be informative, although inconclusive results remain possible. Explain what it could establish and what would require further evidence [@emasmall2006].

These recommendations draw on the EMA guideline on clinical trials in small populations (2006) and FDA rare-disease guidance (final, 2023). The FDA natural-history (2019) and external-control (2023) documents cited here are draft guidance, rather than final recommendations. These sources concern medicinal-product development; use the principles that fit your own study's purpose and discuss alternative designs with a methodological collaborator.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-rare-disease-threshold">
<summary>Common misconception: rare diseases require a different significance threshold</summary>

Rarity does not, by itself, justify increasing the Type I error rate. Alternative designs and error targets need prospective justification; a small available population does not make uncertain evidence more conclusive [@emasmall2006].

</details>

## What can you do when information is limited? {#pilot-feasibility .advanced-heading}



Suppose a team wants to test a new rehabilitation pathway but has little evidence about the treatment effect. It can recruit 40 patients over three months for a feasibility study. Rather than assuming a large improvement to obtain an affordable efficacy calculation, it asks whether recruitment, delivery and follow-up can work in practice.

First check systematic reviews, relevant previous studies, routine service data and clinical expertise. Record the population, outcome, time point and uncertainty of each source. Agree the main trial's clinically meaningful outcome with patients and clinicians. The pilot can investigate recruitment and retention, measurement procedures, acceptability and variability; its noisy treatment estimate should not become the sole basis of the definitive study [@albers2018].

For the pilot, state the resources and the decisions they must support. Here the hypothetical cap is 40 participants, and expected completion of follow-up is 80%. If 32 of 40 complete follow-up, what would that tell the team about retention?

```{r pilot-retention}
pilot_retention <- single_proportion_interval(events = 32, n = 40,
  confidence = .95)
pilot_retention
```

```{r pilot-retention-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Completed follow-up`="32/40 (80%)", `95% Wilson confidence interval`=paste(percent(pilot_retention$lower), "to", percent(pilot_retention$upper)), check.names=FALSE), caption="Retention and its uncertainty in a 40-participant feasibility study.")
```

The observed 80% retention still has a wide interval. Compare it with a prospectively agreed progression criterion and consider reasons for missing outcomes. A point estimate of 80% alone cannot establish that the main trial will retain at least 80%.

Your pilot size should reflect the decision it must support. Ying and colleagues distinguish estimating feasibility with useful precision, assessing progression criteria, detecting practical problems and informing variability for the main trial [@ying2025]. You should specify each outcome's denominator: retention concerns participants enrolled, while a recruitment percentage may concern eligible people approached. Forty enrolled patients do not supply forty observations for every feasibility outcome.

::: {.activity}
Plan a feasibility decision. Before seeing retention results, specify an unacceptable level, a desirable level and what would lead to proceeding, amending or stopping. Compare the intervals for 40 and 80 participants. Explain whether either sample supplies useful information for those decisions, alongside acceptability and reasons for missing follow-up. These criteria need clinical and operational justification, not an arbitrary percentage.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-pilot-progression">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

One possible set of prospectively specified criteria would treat retention below 70% as unacceptable and 80% as desirable. A team could proceed if the estimate is at least 80%, the lower 95% confidence limit exceeds 70%, and delivery and acceptability are satisfactory; amend the pathway if the interval still includes unacceptable retention; and stop or substantially redesign it if the interval lies below 70%. These illustrative thresholds and rules need clinical and operational justification before the results are seen.

For 32/40 retained participants, the 95% Wilson interval is `r percent(wilson_interval(.80, 40)[1, 1])` to `r percent(wilson_interval(.80, 40)[1, 2])`; for 64/80 it is `r percent(wilson_interval(.80, 80)[1, 1])` to `r percent(wilson_interval(.80, 80)[1, 2])`. The 40-person result would lead to amendment or further investigation under these illustrative rules. The 80-person result just meets the numerical progression rule using the unrounded lower limit, but the reasons for missing follow-up and acceptability would still matter. Neither result establishes that true retention is at least 80%. Recruiting 80 would also need its own feasible time and resource plan.

</details>

:::

For another objective, suppose a practical problem independently affects 10% of participants. The chance of observing at least one problem in $n$ participants is $1-(1-0.10)^n$; 29 give at least a 95% chance. This calculation answers a problem-detection question, not an efficacy question, and cannot reliably detect much rarer problems. Observing none does not prove that the problem never occurs [@ying2025]. Different pilot objectives can therefore imply different numbers.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-pilot-goal">
<summary>Common misconception: every pilot needs a treatment-effect power calculation</summary>

A pilot may primarily investigate recruitment, retention or whether procedures are workable. Its numbers should support those feasibility questions and the precision needed for decisions, rather than a universal minimum per arm. A small pilot's uncertain treatment-effect estimate should not become the sole basis for planning the definitive trial [@albers2018].

</details>

[Activity: Pilot study: estimate retention](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pilot_feasibility). It starts with a fixed total of 40 and anticipated retention of 80%. Compare illustrative intervals at 40 and 80 observations; make clear whether another recruitment period or collaboration could obtain the larger sample. This is descriptive estimation of retention, not a treatment-effect power calculation.

Before writing the protocol, you should check relevant guidance and the current funder's requirements. For examples, [NIHR HTA guidance on feasibility and pilot studies](https://njl-admin.nihr.ac.uk/document/download/2023130) distinguishes feasibility questions from definitive efficacy questions; this is an archived guidance example. The [CONSORT extension for randomized pilot and feasibility trials](https://www.bmj.com/content/355/bmj.i5239) asks for a rationale for pilot numbers and criteria for progression [@nihrfeasibility; @eldridge2016]. Reporting guidance helps you document the design; it does not supply one sample-size formula for every study.

# Test your reasoning {#exercises .core-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Justify a planning goal in a new clinical case.
- Assess what a fixed sample can establish.
- Turn your evidence and assumptions into a complete study-planning report.
:::

## Discharge rates {#discharge .core-heading}



Standard care discharges 80% of patients by a specified time point. Suppose comparable evidence suggests an 18-percentage-point expected difference (98% versus 80%), use a more conservative 16-percentage-point target difference (96% versus 80%), and patients judge an 8-percentage-point benefit worthwhile. Consider a 20% relative increase, an alternative target difference of 10 percentage points, and a higher power target. You can use the planning method in [Two proportions](#two-proportions), with the same rounding rule.

Before revealing the answers:

1. Convert each effect to a treatment probability.
2. Predict which scenario needs the most participants.
3. Calculate the per-group and total sample sizes.
4. Explain why the analysis method must be stated, especially with probabilities near one.

<details>
<summary>Show the calculation and interpretation</summary>

```{r discharge-answers}
discharge <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("20% relative increase", "10 percentage points", "Higher power"),
  control = .80, treatment = c(.80 * 1.20, .80 + .10, .80 * 1.20),
  power = c(.80, .80, .90))
discharge$per_group <- mapply(function(p, power) {
  sample_size_two_proportions(p, .80, alpha = .05, power = power)
}, discharge$treatment, discharge$power)
discharge$total <- 2 * discharge$per_group
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(discharge, c("control", "treatment", "power")),
  caption = "Analyzable discharge-study sample sizes using the normal planning approximation in power.prop.test().")
```

The treatment percentages are 96%, 90% and 96%. The approximate totals are `r paste(discharge$total, collapse = ", ")`, respectively. Each per-group count is rounded up before doubling for the total. The expected difference remains 18 points and the clinical threshold remains 8 points in each comparison.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-percentage-points">
<summary>Common misconception: percentages and percentage points are interchangeable</summary>

From a baseline of 80%, a 20% relative increase gives 96% ($0.80\times1.20=0.96$), an increase of 16 percentage points. An increase of 20 percentage points gives 100%. State the baseline and whether the change is relative or absolute before entering event rates into a calculator.

</details>

These planning results use the same approximation as the [reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=discharge). Simulated performance can help you assess whether the approximation is adequate for the proposed event rates and sample size.

[Activity: Open the discharge activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=discharge). The 80% versus 96% scenario starts with 80% target power. Consider whether an outcome so close to 100% makes the simple approximation adequate, and examine simulated performance. A shorter time-to-discharge outcome or clustered ward allocation would require a different method.

</details>

## A fixed total of 70 patients {.advanced-heading}



Suppose only 70 patients can be recruited. Explain what can be learned without treating this limit as evidence that the study has adequate power. Address the intended goal, expected losses, achievable precision and plausible effects. Propose either a defensible revised design or a narrower study purpose.

## Write a sample size justification {.core-heading}



Your 300–600-word justification should cover the clinical question, primary outcome, evidence for assumptions, clinical threshold, target difference, planned analysis, Type I error rate, target power, per-group counts, recruitment inflation and feasibility. It should include a sensitivity table or curve and explain the consequences of uncertain assumptions. The core task does not require a simulation.

You can use the chronic pain report you have developed through the tutorial, or a justified two-arm case of your own. Your explanation should address the target difference's importance and realism, rather than list inputs without their sources. The report should identify the calculation method and distinguish required analyzable counts from recruitment. These elements follow DELTA² and CONSORT's sample size reporting guidance [@cook2018delta2; @consortee2025].

Complete the [student case template](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/case-studies/student_case_template.html) or [Activity: Record and justify your assumptions](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=assumptions_report), and use the core [assessment rubric](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/teaching/assessment_rubric.html) for feedback. For an advanced estimation, feasibility or fixed-dataset project, replace the treatment-power requirement with its relevant information target and denominator.

You can discuss these review questions with a collaborator:

- Are the assumptions supported and distinguished from clinical judgments?
- Does the calculation match the planned analysis?
- Are per-group, total and recruitment counts unambiguous?
- Does the sensitivity analysis keep the appropriate quantities fixed?
- Does the interpretation acknowledge what an inconclusive result could mean?

For an advanced extension, add a simulation result with its generating assumptions, analysis, seed, repetition count and Monte Carlo interval. Explain what it adds to the analytical calculation. You can also write a short hypothetical study abstract that distinguishes the planned design, realized results and interpretation, following the broader learning sequence used in DICE [@thiesmeier2024].

<div class="core-next">Continue along the core route: <a href="#record-assumptions">Record and justify your assumptions</a>.</div>

## Plan your own study {#own-study .advanced-heading}



The statistical, clinical, ethical and logistic questions introduced earlier should help you assess your own project. [Activity: Build your own study calculation](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=own_study) and complete the [case and assumption map](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/case-studies/student_case_template.html). Use hypothetical or public values for this exercise; do not put patient records into the teaching app.

1. Describe the question and design. State the population, comparison, outcome and time point. Check [the study-design guide](#study-designs): one independent observation per person, paired observations, clustered recruitment and prediction models have different planning needs.
2. Choose what the study should establish. Specify an effect to test, a useful interval width, feasibility criteria, or what an already fixed sample could establish. Record evidence sources and plausible alternatives, rather than entering unsupported numbers.
3. Connect clinical and ethical value to the design. Who judges the benefit worthwhile? What burden, harm or opportunity cost would participation bring? What would you do if the likely interval still included both trivial and important effects? A sample meeting a conventional power target does not answer all these questions.
4. Assess resources and communicate a recommendation. State recruitment rate, period, per-person cost and expected losses. Distinguish available recruitment from expected analyzable counts. Explore sensitivity at the original planned n and justify proceeding, collaborating, redesigning, narrowing the aim, or not proceeding. Save the assumptions, method and explanation with the app results.

```{r study-design-help, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat(readLines("../student-materials/study-design-guide.md", warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8"),
  sep = "\n")
```

The diagnostic, prediction and preclinical resources above are also listed in the tutorial references [@stard2015; @riley2020; @tripodai2024; @arrive2020].

# Reproducibility and further reading {#appendix .advanced-heading}



::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Reproduce a calculation or simulation using its inputs, method and random seed.
- Explain why results from different software must be compared using matching assumptions and methods.
:::

The current open edition uses reproducible R plots, tables and browser apps. Compare hypotheses, tests, allocation, continuity corrections and rounding before comparing results across software. Numerical agreement is informative only when the methods and inputs match; methodological validation records belong with the source documentation.

In the chronic pain example, $P_1=0.60$ and $P_2=0.30$. Thus $P_2-P_1=-0.30$, with absolute difference 0.30. Swapping group labels changes the sign, not the power of the same two-sided test.

## Reproduce or adapt the examples {.advanced-heading}

The code uses base R and the shared clinical simulation functions. The two-proportion analysis is a pooled score test without continuity correction, with Newcombe-Wilson confidence intervals. Normal-outcome examples assume independent normal observations with a common variance and use a pooled t test. Binary analytical power is a normal approximation; simulation estimates the finite-sample rejection rate of the specified test.

The shared functions are supplied in `../R/sample_size_functions.R`. Presentation helpers are in `../R/tutorial_helpers.R`. The same clinical simulation functions underpin the [existing OER lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_simulation). A compact demonstration of the repeated-trial algorithm is:

```{r algorithm, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(20260921)  # Once before the batch, not inside the repetitions
B <- 5000
n <- 60
treatment_count <- rbinom(B, n, .60)
control_count <- rbinom(B, n, .30)
results <- analyse_binary(treatment_count, control_count, n, alpha = .05)
mean(results$p_value < .05)
```

The general simulation principle is also described by @lakenscaldwell2021. That paper's factorial examples are not prerequisites for these clinical activities.

For adaptation, keep the editable R Markdown, shared case settings, app code and build instructions alongside the rendered tutorial. Review changes to assumptions and methods together with the resulting figures and activities. This follows the computational-resource development approach described by @bothmann2021; its manuscript is a development perspective rather than evidence of learning gains. See the [adaptation guide](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/teaching/adaptation_guide.html) for practical steps.

## Further planning approaches {#further-planning-approaches .advanced-heading}

The core calculations evaluate power at specified values. More specialized approaches account for additional uncertainty or a different research objective:

- Safeguard power uses uncertainty in a previous difference estimate when planning. It can imply a much larger sample when the evidence is weak; it does not establish clinical importance [@perugini2014].
- Bayesian and hybrid approaches can average performance over a justified distribution of plausible parameter values. Assurance or expected power answers a different question from power at one fixed difference; the distribution and decision rule need justification [@kunzmann2021review; @pezeshk2003].
- Mixed-model simulation can represent clustered or repeated observations and the intended analysis, but needs credible dependency assumptions, convergence checks and sensitivity analysis [@pargent2024].
- Multiple outcomes or treatment comparisons need a prespecified success rule and appropriate error control. Power for each comparison separately does not establish the probability that all required comparisons succeed [@fong2026].

These are extensions to discuss with a methodological collaborator, not automatic ways to reduce recruitment. For design-specific methods, use [Where does my study fit?](#study-designs) and the references below.

## About this resource {-}

This tutorial builds on Katalin Tamási's original e-learning module [@tamasi2021]. The presentation and three simulation activities are inspired by chapters 1, 11 and 15 of *Power Analysis with Superpower* [@superpowerbook2022], and some clinical scenarios are based on the ideas of Carlotta Drewer and Bert van der Leest. The clinical explanations, activities and figures here are tailored to this tutorial. Hans Burgerhof's *Statistics 3: Sample size calculation* e-learning module also informs the discussion of testing and estimation goals [@burgerhof2020].

The development of the epidemiology and medical statistics e-learning environment is described by @wieringa2025. Our account of identifying learner and teacher needs provides background for involving students in reviewing this open edition and combining independent preparation with guided discussion.

Further statistical background comes from @clayton2019, @kirkwood2003, @whitley2002, @pourhoseingholi2013 and @wang2020.

Original teaching materials are shared under CC BY 4.0 and original code under MIT; see the [reuse and citation guidance](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/documentation/reuse-and-citation.html) for attribution and third-party exceptions. Obtain consent before publishing student work, identifiable feedback or named student acknowledgments. This consent requirement concerns student contributions, rather than reuse of the licensed teaching materials.

The [teaching guide](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/teaching/TEACHING_GUIDE.html), [case template](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/case-studies/student_case_template.html) and [assessment rubric](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/teaching/assessment_rubric.html) support classroom use.

## Further reading {-}

Your choice of reading can follow the decision you need to make; the [reading guide](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/documentation/reading-guide.html) connects these sources to the activities.

- @fong2026 and @zrineh2026 introduce clinical planning; @lakens2022 explains alternative sample size justifications; @cook2018delta2 supports choosing and reporting a target difference. Apply these to the assumptions report.
- Design-specific guidance: @ying2025 and @eldridge2016 address pilot objectives; @candel2023 addresses efficient designs; @riley2020 addresses prediction-model development. CONSORT's explanation and elaboration details reporting, including sample size assumptions in item 16a [@consortee2025].
- Advanced methods and reference books: @pargent2024 explains mixed-model simulation, and @superpowerbook2022 supports exploring repeated studies. @julious2004 reviews normal-outcome trial calculations; @julious2023 provides broader design-specific sample size methods. @piantadosi2024 places planning within broader trial methodology. These books are references rather than prerequisites.

For readers exploring prediction models, @shamsutdinova2026 describes recent simulation-based approaches (currently in preprint).
